###### ✦

----------
Good morning, founders 🕶️

Every startup keeps two balance sheets. There's the one your accountant keeps, and there's the real one: **whatever someone will pay for, or walk off with.** EasyA found sponsors willing to prepay for its users, so it never needed a VC. OpenAI says an engineer left for Apple carrying 100+ confidential files on his last day. And Gallup says 8 in 10 Americans think businesses like yours raise prices just to pad profits. Value gets decided at the edges: at checkout, at renewal and on someone's last day. Which edge are you guarding?

In today's newsletter, we'll get into:

* Two brothers, $1.1B and zero VC dollars

* Apple vs. OpenAI: files out both doors

* Bumble's 138% "premium" on a crushed stock

* Anduril's $90B employee payday


----------###### ✦

----------
* 🛒 Amazon's cut went from ~19% of sales in 2014 to close to half for Not-Ship's example apparel seller using its fulfillment and ads. [Add up every Amazon fee](https://www.not-ship.com/how-amazon-pushes-up-prices-all-across-the-internet/), then check your own-site price: undercutting Amazon can cost you the Buy Box.

* 🧾 8 in 10 Americans think businesses overcharge, and 74% want firms to accept lower profits instead, so [show the cost driver and the math](https://www.inc.com/henna-pryor/8-in-10-americans-think-businesses-raise-prices-more-than-necessary-thats-a-believability-problem/91418338) with every price hike.

* 📈 Nearly 1 in 4 finance firms tie raises, bonuses or promotions to AI skills, a Selby Jennings survey of 500 executives found. Add one question to your reviews, ["how did you use AI, and what changed?"](https://live.euronext.com/en/financial-news/wall-street-firms-tie-bonuses-promotions-ai-skills-survey-finds), and reward results, not usage.

* 🧭 a16z maps three ways to sell an AI agent: Service closes fastest on existing outsourcing budgets, Platform has more pricing upside but longer cycles, and Full-Stack keeps the most upside and the compliance headache. [Pick the motion that fits your constraint](https://a16z.com/winning-the-relay-race-long-running-agents-in-high-value-customer-journeys/); even a16z says it's "too early to tell."

## Five bullets of updates

1. 🎙️ **Flock CEO Garrett Langley said onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt that the company's gunshot-detection microphones hear "just gunshots," while Flock's website advertises alerts for street takeovers, crashes, fireworks and sideshows.** A spokesperson later confirmed the broader list. Before your next keynote, [check your stage claims against your own FAQ](https://techcrunch.com/2026/10/14/flock-ceo-says-its-microphones-detect-just-gunshots-its-website-says-different/), because reporters already will have.

2. 💔 **Bumble agreed to go private with Ithaca Holdings for about $1.3B in cash, or $6.05 a share, a 138% premium to its pre-talks close, five years after listing at $14B.** That "premium" sits on a stock flattened by a 15.2% revenue drop and 16.4% fewer paying users last quarter, so [pressure-test your exit options](https://thenextweb.com/news/bumble-ithaca-holdings-1-3bn-deal) while your growth line still points up.

3. 🔥 **CoreWeave shares fell 15.5% as the yield on its 2032 bonds hit about 14.8%, while CEO Mike Intrator's memo insisted its backlog "more than supports all of our debt obligations."** If you've signed or prepaid multi-year GPU capacity with a neocloud, [ask for termination and continuity terms](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/14/coreweave-stock-bond-yields-ai-debt.html) now, while your supplier still wants your signature.

4. 🪖 **Anduril opened an employee tender at $94.80 a share, valuing the defense startup at roughly $90B, capped at $1.3B and running October 13 to November 9.** That's up from $61B in May, nearly 50% in five months. A [tender works as retention liquidity](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/14/anduril-tender-offer-valuation.html) you can price before your next round, and it gives your best people a reason not to go job-hunting.

5. 📱 **Google is reportedly auto-linking your phone number to every Google account signed in on your Android device, including work and secondary profiles, according to Android Authority and a Reddit thread.** It's a five-minute fix: switch off ["Verify phone numbers automatically"](https://www.androidauthority.com/google-auto-phone-number-verification-android-3723117/) in Android's Google settings, then remove your number from each work account by hand.

### **EasyA's users pay nothing. Google and Ripple pay first**

View image: (https://media4.giphy.com/media/v1.Y2lkPTI0NTBlYzMwbWg2cWFrYXN0aGt2YmI3dGpwaXA0eWQwcXlnOG1xdnR0cDFvbWlpdSZlcD12MV9naWZzX3NlYXJjaCZjdD1n/HVqwn3AZLXMZhgis6H/giphy.gif) [Happy GIF by The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon]
Follow image link: (https://startupclub.slidebean.com/)
Caption: Gif by fallontonight on Giphy

Most startups raise money to find customers. _EasyA_ found customers who'd pay to meet its users, and skipped the raise.

**The receipt:** brothers _Phil and Dom Kwok_ say they've kept **100%** of the company and run it with **30 employees**. They also say an independent valuation puts it at **$1.1 billion**. Its **1.3 million** users pay nothing. A direct listing is planned for the first half of _2027_, and a draft registration is with the SEC.

#### **So who's actually paying?**

Platforms that need developers. _Google_, _Ripple_ and others pay [EasyA](https://www.easya.io/about) to feature their coding challenges in its app and at its hackathons. A partner like _Ripple_ says how many developers and startups it wants building on its tech, and EasyA goes and finds them. The founders say contracts run from **mid six to mid seven figures**, last multiple years and are billed semi-annually or annually, upfront.

Think of it as a developer-relations department for rent, where the tenant pays before moving in. Cash lands before costs do. That's the money a seed round would buy, minus the board seat.

It wasn't plan A. A **£10-a-month** subscription (about **$15**) flopped, and selling to schools pushed revenue close to zero. The fix came in _2022_: one San Francisco hackathon, roughly **70 developers**, and the realization that the sponsors were the customer. Even the exit skips the raise. A direct listing lets existing shareholders sell without the company issuing new stock.

#### **So what's the founder takeaway?**

Before you raise, list the companies that profit when your users succeed. A dev tool's users matter to cloud providers. A freelancer app's users matter to banks and accounting software. Then sell those companies a prepaid sponsorship: a committed number of outcomes, multi-year, billed upfront.

Watch for the public registration ahead of the _2027_ listing. That's when "the founders say" turns into audited numbers anyone can read.

Read the source (https://www.inc.com/tobi-opeyemi-amure/easya-ai-billion-company-venture-capital-customers-upfront-funding/91418821)

### **Apple says OpenAI took its secrets. **
**OpenAI says: same**

View image: (https://media4.giphy.com/media/v1.Y2lkPTI0NTBlYzMwM3A5YWd3am9xdXZyd3BvcTI3OGFkdDF3YjRnZWpiYTc2aTAzdXkzdyZlcD12MV9naWZzX3NlYXJjaCZjdD1n/l36kU80xPf0ojG0Erg/giphy.gif) [Blaming Spider-Man GIF]
Follow image link: (https://startupclub.slidebean.com/)
Caption: Giphy

The Hollywood version writes itself: a scrappy AI lab raids the trillion-dollar hardware giant, and the giant sues. The filings are messier, and more useful.

_Apple_ **[sued ](https://thenextweb.com/news/apple-openai-trade-secrets-hearing)**_**[OpenAI](https://thenextweb.com/news/apple-openai-trade-secrets-hearing)**_**[ in ](https://thenextweb.com/news/apple-openai-trade-secrets-hearing)**_**[July](https://thenextweb.com/news/apple-openai-trade-secrets-hearing)**_, alleging its hardware chief _Tang Tan_ and former iPhone engineer _Chang Liu_ coordinated to pull Apple's confidential product information out through hires. On Wednesday, Judge _Edward Davila_ said he's **"highly likely"** to grant Apple an injunction barring OpenAI from using it, Bloomberg Law reported. Likely. Not decided.

Then OpenAI flipped the script. Its new filing alleges that an engineer who joined from Apple, stayed **six months** and went back sent **100+ highly confidential files** about an unreleased OpenAI device to his personal accounts on _June 2_, his last day. It says he then presented OpenAI's plans to Apple's senior leadership. Apple says it found no evidence and calls the filing a distraction.

#### **Who's claiming what?**

Apple says Liu exploited an authentication flaw to reach its network storage and download files. OpenAI's filings say Apple encouraged staff to use personal iCloud for work, and that Apple's own authentication error left Liu with access. Apple's lawyer, in court: "They don't have 400 bad apples, your honor, they have a few bad apples."

**Here's the part that matters for you:** whoever's right, both stories run through the same door. A departing employee, a personal account, and access that outlived the job.

#### **Why not just make people sign a non-compete?**

Because California voids them. Apple can't stop an engineer from leaving. It can only try to prove theft afterward. If the two best-lawyered companies on earth are stuck there, "we trust our team" is not a security policy.

**So here's your move:** audit offboarding this week. Kill auto-forwarding to personal email, revoke access the day someone leaves, and ban work files in personal cloud storage. Ten minutes of IT now beats a forensic image later.

Watch for Davila's ruling and any OpenAI counterclaim. OpenAI's reported first device, a **$300-plus** doughnut-shaped speaker due in _2027_, now ships with a lawsuit attached.
